item.title: Los Angeles Prosecutor to Oversee Inquiry Into Mar-a-Lago Search
item.description:
The Justice Department has chosen Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, to oversee a key aspect of the so-called grand conspiracy case in Florida that has been scrutinizing Obama-era officials who have investigated President Trump, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Mr. Essayli will focus narrowly on the question of whether agents and prosecutors broke the law four years ago when they searched Mar-a-Lago, Mr. Trump’s private club and residence in Florida, the people said. The search was an early step in what ultimately led to an indictment of Mr. Trump by the special counsel Jack Smith on charges of mishandling classified documents and obstructing the government’s repeated efforts to retrieve them.

The decision to have Mr. Essayli work on an investigation into the Mar-a-Lago search was the latest shake-up in the grand conspiracy case, a crucial aspect of the president’s retribution campaign that has been plagued for months by a lack of focus and a wave of firings and resignations.

It also suggested that the central theory of the case — that the various investigations into Mr. Trump over the past 10 years or so were part of a single conspiracy to hurt his political prospects — may not be legally viable. Having tried for months to prove that Mr. Smith and other law enforcement officials were part of an overarching plot against Mr. Trump, prosecutors now appear to be pursuing smaller and separate lines of inquiry.

The move held personal significance for Mr. Essayli as well. Last month, a federal judge ruled that he has been illegally serving in his post in Los Angeles after remaining in the job beyond the 120-day limit set by law for acting U.S. attorneys. The Justice Department has said it will appeal that ruling, and a department official said Mr. Essayli will continue working in Los Angeles while also overseeing the investigation into the Mar-a-Lago search.

A spokesman for Mr. Essayli did not respond to messages seeking comment.

In recent weeks, the inquiry into the search has largely focused on efforts to get information from a group of former F.B.I. agents who took part in it. The former agents — many of whom were fired for having taken part in the classified documents case — received subpoenas this summer to appear before a grand jury in Federal District Court in Fort Pierce, Fla., on the theory that they might be able to offer evidence that the search was conducted illegally.

But lawyers for the former agents threw cold water on that theory in September. They asserted in court papers that if their clients were forced to testify in front of the grand jury, they would say that the search of Mar-a-Lago — like other aspects of the classified documents prosecution — was conducted fairly and in keeping with the law.

The lawyers raised another potential obstacle to their clients’ providing testimony: The judge who oversaw the classified documents case, Aileen M. Cannon, has barred Mr. Smith and members of his team from publicly discussing details of the investigation contained in a report about the case that was submitted after its conclusion. The lawyers have asked Judge Cannon whether the former agents can discuss the case in front of the grand jury without violating her order, but she has not yet issued a decision.

When the grand conspiracy investigation began late last year, the Justice Department seemed to be swinging for the fences in its efforts to appease Mr. Trump’s desire for revenge against a wide array of his most reviled opponents.

The inquiry initially sought to go after not only Mr. Smith but also other officials who tried to hold Mr. Trump accountable in other criminal inquiries. Chief among them were John O. Brennan, the former C.I.A. director, and James B. Comey, who ran the F.B.I. during Mr. Trump’s first term. Both men played important roles in the investigation into potential ties between Russia and Mr. Trump’s 2016 campaign.

But the broad investigation ran into a series of roadblocks — not least that there was little evidence that Mr. Smith, Mr. Brennan and Mr. Comey had actually conspired with one another. There were also seemingly insurmountable legal problems with seeking to connect events that occurred in different places — Washington and Florida, for example — over nearly a decade.

The first prosecutor who looked at the case, focusing on issues surrounding Mr. Brennan, was removed from the inquiry after she determined that there was no viable path toward bringing an indictment.

Other prosecutors stepped down in the months that ensued — including Joseph diGenova, a longtime Trump loyalist who was brought into the case this spring, promising to bring charges quickly. Two weeks ago, after the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections, Jason A. Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida who was nominally in charge of the investigation, also resigned amid growing dissatisfaction with his performance by his bosses in Washington.

Even before the midterms, the Justice Department had quietly signaled that it was no longer actively seeking to prove a grand conspiracy against Mr. Trump, but would instead carve out smaller prosecutions against his perceived enemies where it could.

Case in point: Prosecutors who had been working on the grand conspiracy case were instrumental in filing charges against Mr. Comey in Washington last month, accusing him of mishandling sensitive national security information that was published in an article in The New York Times.

item.title: Lawmakers’ Data Is Vulnerable to Trump’s Justice Department, Senator Warns
item.description:
A Democratic senator is urging Congress to secure lawmakers’ phone calls, emails and video meetings from the executive branch as President Trump threatens criminal investigations targeting members who conduct overly aggressive oversight of his administration.

The risk of retaliatory surveillance by the Justice Department, which could chill or blunt oversight as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress after the midterms, is a concern in part because many lawmakers use campaign-provided phones and personal email accounts for official business. Prosecutors have repeatedly subpoenaed communications companies for lawmakers’ records.

Senator Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, said the Trump administration’s “threats to investigate members of Congress who do our job and oversee the executive branch are a five-alarm warning that the Senate needs to ramp up the security of our communications as soon as possible.”

The warning dovetails with concerns cited in a Senate report last week about “the threat of hacking and cyberattacks on senators and staff on their official and personal devices and accounts.” It directed the sergeant-at-arms office, the chamber’s technology provider, to study how “to provide end to end encrypted voice, video and text communications,” including storing data on its servers.

Lawmakers’ communications and data have repeatedly proved vulnerable.

One threat: foreign espionage. In 2024, Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, then the majority leader, was among political leaders whose phones were targeted by Salt Typhoon, a Chinese hacking group that penetrated American telecommunications networks and surveilled the calls and texts of high-profile victims.

Criminal investigations pose another threat. During leak inquiries in the first Trump term, the Justice Department secretly obtained “non-content communications records for phone numbers and email addresses” of two Democratic lawmakers and dozens of aides from both parties, and “sought records of a Republican member of Congress,” according to an inspector general report.

In 2022 and 2023, prosecutors examining Mr. Trump’s attempt to subvert the 2020 election secretly subpoenaed phone logs of 20 current and former Republican lawmakers who had spoken with Mr. Trump or his proxies as they pushed allies to block certification of Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory around the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol. Those call logs, or “toll records,” show who communicated with whom and when, but not what was said.

As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and vow to investigate Mr. Trump and his inner circle, the administration has threatened criminal investigations in retaliation for oversight it deems unduly aggressive — raising the possibility that it could seize lawmakers’ communications and records.

Mr. Trump’s White House counsel, Will Scharf, warned that subpoenas deemed to lack a valid legislative purpose “may cross the line into blatant criminality” and “may warrant further investigation.” Aaron Reitz, a U.S. attorney in Texas, sent letters to Democratic lawmakers accusing them of planning to abuse oversight powers, citing civil rights crimes and demanding they preserve records and communications.

Any such attempted prosecution is unlikely to succeed because the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause gives Congress immunity for legislative acts. Still, the administration has repeatedly investigated Mr. Trump’s perceived adversaries on dubious legal and factual grounds, and exposed confidential law enforcement information to embarrass them.

In February, a grand jury rebuffed the Justice Department’s bid to indict several congressional Democrats for making a video reminding troops of their duty to disobey illegal orders. The White House released F.B.I. files last summer showing a former Democratic congressman whom Mr. Trump dislikes had confidentially admitted to agents a decade ago that he had sex with a woman who turned out to be a suspected Chinese spy.

The vulnerability of lawmakers’ communications records stems from ethics rules and gaps in federal law, said Christopher Soghoian, a technologist who recently left Mr. Wyden’s staff after a decade working on surveillance and cybersecurity.

Ethics rules prohibit lawmakers from using congressional resources to conduct campaign business like soliciting donations but allow official business using campaign resources. Most therefore use campaign-provided phones and consumer email accounts for all their communications — even as aides use work phones and government email addresses, he said.

“We have the 100 most important people in the Senate using cellphones and email accounts that are completely outside the perimeter, and the institution can’t protect them — it’s bananas,” Mr. Soghoian said. “Work-related communications of the entire institution are sitting on Yahoo or Google servers.”

Each chamber controls its own technology, and there appears to be little appetite for outside scrutiny of a widespread practice that invites awkward comparison to the scandal over Hillary Clinton’s use of a private email server to conduct official business as secretary of state. The sergeant-at-arms office did not respond to inquiries, including how many senators, if any, use Senate-provided phones. Its House counterpart’s spokeswoman declined to comment.

In 2020, as Senate offices increasingly used cloud services like Google Documents and Slack on their own, the Senate inserted a provision into a bill adding some protections. The resulting statute allows Senate offices to ask courts to quash legal demands for their data and permits providers to disregard gag orders and notify Senate offices of such directives.

But major gaps remain. The law does not cover the House. It does not require companies to notify the Senate of such subpoenas, and senators cannot challenge directives they do not know about. Its text is ambiguous about coverage of campaign phones and private email accounts, and it created no system to alert companies when lawmakers are using those.

The Senate sergeant-at-arms office has sought to address some weaknesses by contractually requiring providers to notify the chamber of data demands. But a May 2025 letter from Mr. Wyden to colleagues warned that “significant gaps remain, especially for the campaign and personal phones used by most senators.”

Later in 2025, after revelations that prosecutors investigating Mr. Trump’s attempted subversion of the 2020 election had subpoenaed the phone logs of several Republican lawmakers, senators slipped a measure expanding the 2020 law into a bill ending a government shutdown. It required notification and clarified coverage of senators’ campaign and personal lines.

But it also allowed senators whose phone records were obtained without notice to sue and automatically collect $500,000 in taxpayer funds per record. It would have applied retroactively, creating a windfall for Mr. Trump’s Senate allies — though not his House ones. After a backlash, Congress repealed the entire measure, reopening the gaps.

At a February Senate oversight hearing on the election-case subpoenas, telecom lawyers testified that their companies had created a system to identify Senate-commissioned lines. They said they would notify Congress of subpoenas when possible and challenge nondisclosure orders in court.

They said they were working with the Senate sergeant-at-arms office to identify campaign and personal numbers used by lawmakers. But Mr. Soghoian described a haphazard system, with some Senate offices emailing telecom lobbyists their bosses’ numbers — meaning companies likely still do not know all the accounts that should set off notices if subpoenaed.

He also warned of broader threats. State and local prosecutors seeking political prominence could subpoena communications companies for congressional records. And while reports of spyware on legislators’ phones are common abroad, he said, they are rare in the United States because no one systematically looks for it.

Mr. Wyden has urged his colleagues to allow the sergeant-at-arms office to provide cybersecurity help for lawmakers’ campaign phones and personal online accounts, and to provide encrypted video and audio meeting software. That conversation has largely unfolded outside public view.

“I and other members have repeatedly urged Senate leaders — as recently as this summer — to secure our communications against surveillance by spies, criminals and the executive branch,” Mr. Wyden said.

item.title: The Secret History of a 1972 Case on Press Freedom
item.description:
This week’s Docket is a little different. As The New York Times celebrates its 175th anniversary, I interviewed the author of a new book on a fascinating case that pitted the F.B.I. against the Black Panthers and, for a time, The Times against one of its own reporters.

In the case, Branzburg v. Hayes in 1972, the Supreme Court rejected a constitutional privilege for reporters to protect confidential sources by a 5-to-4 vote. I wrote about the case back in July, exploring its implications for subpoenas the Trump administration tried to issue this summer to some of my colleagues.

In the new book, Lee Levine wrote about the history of the case and about Earl Caldwell, the reporter at its center. He drew on The Times’s archives, the justices’ papers, as well as records from the Nixon White House, the Justice Department and the F.B.I.

Levine’s history, “In Bad Faith: Earl Caldwell and the Fight for a Free Press,” takes a fair-minded but unflinching look at the tensions between Caldwell, a Black reporter who covered the Black Panthers, and The Times’s lawyers, management and editors.

This interview with Levine, who represented The Times and many other news organizations when he was a media lawyer, has been lightly edited.

Tell me a little about Earl Caldwell.

Earl was one of the first Black journalists hired by the mainstream news media to report on the urban riots of the 1960s. In 1968, he was the only journalist at the Lorraine Motel when Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated. Earl’s vivid account led The Times’s coverage.

A few months later, he was dispatched to Oakland to cover the Black Panther Party, a group of young urban Blacks who had gained a measure of notoriety by arming themselves in response to what they believed to be police brutality and violence.

Nixon’s Justice Department subpoenaed Caldwell. What was its goal?

By the time Caldwell arrived in the Bay Area, the Panthers had become an obsession of J. Edgar Hoover and the F.B.I.

The Panthers were the target of an F.B.I. covert counterintelligence operation designed to neutralize them by imprisoning their leaders, orchestrating the murders of some of them and influencing media coverage of their activities. For Hoover, it was vital that the public believe the Panthers were a violent group of street thugs.

He didn’t know it at the time, but Earl Caldwell stood in Hoover’s way. Earl had worked hard to earn the Panthers’ trust and had been rewarded with unique access to them, leaders and rank-and-file alike. The result was a series of stories in The Times that painted a very different picture of the Black Panther Party than the one Hoover and the newly elected Nixon administration favored.

Although he certainly reported on the extent to which the Panthers had armed themselves, as well as their embrace of the version of communism and revolution championed by Mao Zedong, his stories also brought home to Times readers their commitment to social justice, from their groundbreaking “breakfast for children” program to free medical clinics and other social action designed to benefit inner-city Blacks.

By subpoenaing Caldwell to testify behind the closed doors of the grand jury, the bureau hoped not only to secure his testimony for whatever it might be worth but, more important, to disrupt his relationship with the Panthers and put a stop to his reporting about them.

Caldwell and The Times had separate legal teams. How come? And did they see eye to eye?

After Caldwell was subpoenaed, The Times hired a senior partner at a white-shoe San Francisco law firm to represent him. At their first meeting, the lawyer advised Caldwell to collect up all his notes about the Panthers because, given what he characterized as rampant inner-city violence in the Bay Area, Caldwell would undoubtedly have to produce at least a portion of them to the grand jury.

That was not the news Caldwell expected to hear. With the help of the handful of other Black journalists then working for mainstream news outlets in the Bay Area, he secured pro bono counsel of his own through the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. That lawyer, Anthony Amsterdam, was a highly respected constitutional scholar and he advised Caldwell he had a right, grounded in the First Amendment, to refuse to comply with the subpoena.

The Times — through Jim Goodale, its general counsel; Abe Rosenthal, its top editor; and Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, its publisher — agreed with Amsterdam’s analysis and joined Caldwell in moving to quash the subpoena. The presiding judge agreed as well and ordered that, when Caldwell appeared before the grand jury, the First Amendment authorized him to refuse to reveal any information he had learned in confidence.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

For The Times, this was a momentous victory, the first time a U.S. court had ever held that the First Amendment protects reporters from compelled disclosure of information they receive in confidence.

But Black journalists, both in the Bay Area and across the country, saw things very differently. For them, Caldwell’s appearance before the grand jury, standing alone, would destroy the trust he had earned from the Panthers and would effectively end his ability to report on them. So, on Caldwell’s behalf and to The Times’s consternation, Amsterdam appealed.

The Times did not join him, much to the consternation of Caldwell, the handful of other Black journalists in its newsroom and Black reporters across the country.

The court of appeals ruled in Caldwell’s favor, holding that he had a First Amendment right to refuse even to appear before the grand jury. After the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to intervene, the justices agreed to hear the case, combining it with two others in which, following Caldwell’s victory, reporters had invoked it to resist subpoenas that had been issued to them.

How did the Supreme Court rule?

By a vote of 5 to 4, the court ruled against Caldwell, holding that he was required to appear before the grand jury and, worse still, provide to it any relevant information he might have about their activities whether or not it had been received in confidence. The only exception, Justice Byron White wrote for the court’s majority, would be if a subpoena was issued to a reporter “other than in good faith” for purposes beyond the legitimate needs of law enforcement.

What was Justice William Rehnquist’s role in the case? Did he have a conflict of interest?

Rehnquist took his seat on the Supreme Court just weeks before it heard arguments in the Caldwell case. Immediately before that he had been the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel.

Documents I obtained as a result of a lawsuit Caldwell and I filed against the Justice Department reveal that Rehnquist played a significant role in formulating the department’s position in the case.

He did not, however, recuse himself from participating in the court’s deliberations and, not surprisingly, he was persuaded by the arguments he had a significant hand in crafting.

If Rehnquist had recused himself, the court would have divided evenly and, under its rules, the decision of the court of appeals in Caldwell’s favor would have been affirmed.

What has the impact of the Branzburg decision been?

Although the news media itself proclaimed the decision a major defeat for press freedom, Jim Goodale saw it differently. He mounted a coordinated and vigorous campaign to convince lower courts that, in fact, the court had recognized a First Amendment-based right of journalists to decline to testify about and against their sources in a variety of settings.

For the next 30 years, Goodale’s gambit paid off handsomely, with most courts across the country adopting his view. That changed in the 1990s when Richard Posner, a highly respected appellate judge, took issue with Goodale’s interpretation and insisted that the court had declined to recognize any constitutional right at all. Since then, Posner’s view has become increasingly prevalent, especially in criminal and grand jury proceedings.

Today, the Trump administration is able and more than willing to argue that the grand jury subpoenas it has issued to reporters are invulnerable to constitutional attack. The silver lining for the press may be that even the government must concede that subpoenas issued “other than in good faith” are invalid under the First Amendment.

Despite the Supreme Court’s failure to appreciate the bad faith that infected the subpoena to Earl Caldwell, the Trump administration has made no effort to conceal its motives.

What became of Caldwell?

Caldwell fully expected that, when he maintained his refusal to appear before the grand jury in the face of the Supreme Court’s mandate, he would be imprisoned. He did not anticipate that, following the decision, he would never hear from the government again. Having secured a ruling from the Supreme Court that he and other journalists had no constitutional right to protect their confidences from government subpoenas, the Justice Department and F.B.I. apparently had no further use for either Earl Caldwell or his testimony.

These days, Earl is long retired from journalism. He is in his early 90s and, in recent years, has had some serious health issues. I was able to visit with him a few weeks ago and present him with a copy of the book. It made him smile.

Please send me your comments on protecting sources or anything else at the-docket@nytimes.com. We’re off next week for Thanksgiving. See you in December. — Adam

item.title: Top Massachusetts Court to Weigh Lindsay Clancy’s Motion to Dismiss
item.description:
Massachusetts’s highest court will decide whether the charges against Lindsay Clancy, the woman accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, should be dismissed following the mistrial in her case.

The state’s Supreme Judicial Court said on Thursday that it would hear oral arguments on the matter in January. In a succinct three-page decision, it said it had assessed Ms. Clancy’s appeal and concluded that “review of the merits” of her arguments “by the full court is warranted.”

The finding by the Supreme Judicial Court follows months of arguments by Ms. Clancy’s lawyers that a second trial would violate her right to be protected from double jeopardy. They assert that the trial judge, William Sullivan, failed to properly investigate the lone juror who voted to convict Ms. Clancy, and that the mistrial might have been avoided if the judge had thoroughly looked into the juror’s conduct during deliberations.

Judge Sullivan denied her lawyers’ motion to dismiss the first-degree murder charges on Nov. 9, finding that there had been no legal reason for him to look further into the juror’s conduct.

The judge also denied a separate motion by the defense that asked the court to review the juror’s cellphone records and other background information. Judge Sullivan wrote that such a post-trial inquiry “would be an improper intrusion into this juror’s privacy and would serve to discourage citizens from being willing to serve as jurors in the future.”

After a six-week trial in Plymouth, Mass., which included nearly 40 hours of deliberations, the deadlocked jury could not break its 11-1 impasse. The jury, most of which had voted to find Ms. Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, had complained to the judge that the holdout was refusing to apply the legal standard regarding reasonable doubt.

Judge Sullivan declared the mistrial on Sept. 4.

“We will continue to strongly contend that the trial court made a pivotal error” in declining to dig deeper after the other jurors raised concerns, Martin Weinberg, a lawyer for Ms. Clancy, said in a statement on Thursday.

The office of Timothy Cruz, the district attorney prosecuting Ms. Clancy, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The hearing before the court in Boston early next year will not be the first time the Supreme Judicial Court considers Ms. Clancy’s case. In the final hours before the mistrial was declared in September, her lawyers made a highly unusual, last-ditch effort to prevent it, requesting an emergency hearing before the higher court. A brief online hearing was held before a single justice, who denied the defense request for an investigation of the holdout juror.

Michael Desronvil, the holdout juror, has publicly defended his conduct since the mistrial, stating that he had no doubt about Ms. Clancy’s guilt.

At a hearing on Monday, Judge Sullivan set a date in late March for a second trial. Prosecutors have not clearly stated if they intend to try Ms. Clancy again on first-degree murder charges, but the fact that they agreed to a spring trial date suggests that they may intend to do so. If they opted to reduce the charges, Ms. Clancy’s case could be heard by a judge instead.

Ms. Clancy, 36, has remained in custody at a state hospital since the mistrial. Her lawyer argued during her trial that she was not criminally responsible for killing Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, in January 2023 because she was experiencing severe postpartum mental illness and hallucinated a voice that ordered her to kill them and herself.

item.title: No Charges Filed in Wisconsin Police Shooting That Led to Protests
item.description:
A Madison, Wis., police officer will not face charges in the fatal shooting in July of a man who was wielding a knife, the local district attorney said on Thursday. The death of the man, Corey Ruiz, touched off days of tense protests after video of the shooting circulated widely online.

Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson killed Mr. Ruiz, 38, on July 22 during a confrontation at a busy intersection near the capital city’s downtown.

Officer Baitinger-Peterson was among several officers who responded to reports of a man looking into parked vehicles and possibly attempting a burglary, officials said at the time. The officers approached Mr. Ruiz, who they said fled on a bicycle and then pulled out a knife during a struggle. Officers tried to stop Mr. Ruiz with a Taser, but the device did not incapacitate him, officials said.

Officer Baitinger-Peterson was injured by the knife and fired at Mr. Ruiz, killing him, officials said.

Ismael Ozanne, the Dane County district attorney, on Thursday described Mr. Ruiz’s death as a tragedy in a statement announcing his decision to not bring charges. But after reviewing the evidence, he said, there was no basis to prosecute the officer.

“It was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody,” Mr. Ozanne wrote.

Ben Crump, a lawyer for the Ruiz family, referred to the shooting as an “execution” at a news conference on Thursday and described it as “the textbook definition of excessive use of force.”

“We believe the district attorney should have charged this officer for killing Corey Ruiz,” Mr. Crump added.

Mr. Ruiz was Black, and the shooting renewed concerns about how Black people are treated by the police in Wisconsin and across the country. The shooting took place near where a Madison police officer had shot and killed Anthony Robinson Jr., a 19-year-old Black man, in 2015. In that case, which also led to large protests, Mr. Ozanne found that force was justified, and the officer was not charged.

For several days after Mr. Ruiz’s death, protesters occupied the area near the site of the killing, shutting down traffic and clashing at times with law enforcement.

The police hired Officer Baitinger-Peterson in 2015, and he had worked in several roles for the agency. He did not have a history of using deadly force, officials said. After the shooting, he and the other officers involved were placed on administrative leave.

Family members described Mr. Ruiz as a father who was caring and smart.

Public records showed that he had been convicted of crimes, including theft and resisting or obstructing an officer.

item.title: Senate Republicans Block Bid to Rein in Trump on Iran War
item.description:
Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a measure directing President Trump to end the war with Iran or win congressional approval to continue it, weeks after losing their majority in midterm elections shaped by a voter backlash to the conflict.

The resolution, which passed the House in September by the largest bipartisan margin to date, failed by a vote of 51 to 48.

Since the conflict began on Feb. 28, Congress has collectively held 21 Iran war powers votes, six in the House and 15 in the Senate.

Ashley Wu/The New York Times

It was the first time either chamber had voted on the war since the midterm elections, though it was the 21st such vote since the conflict began in February as Democrats have repeatedly forced the G.O.P. to weigh in on it.

The vote suggested that, while many prominent Republicans have conceded that public antipathy for the war cost them their congressional majorities, the message from the voters had not changed the party’s position on it.

Three Republicans — Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — joined Democrats in support of directing an end to the conflict. Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the lone Democrat to oppose the measure.

Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, has sided with Democrats on similar resolutions but voted no on Thursday.

Mr. Tillis said he did not believe that the nonbinding resolution would do anything to bring about an end to the war, telling reporters after his vote that continuing to pass such resolutions would amount to “feeding a political narrative and not putting any more weight on solving the fundamental problem. That is why I vote the way I vote.”

In the immediate aftermath of Republicans’ widespread electoral losses, party leaders were quick to fault the war and its economic impacts.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance wrote in a lengthy postmortem on social media. Hours later, Mr. Trump said that he mostly agreed with that assessment, but argued that he had had “no choice” but to launch strikes against Iran.

“If I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” he said the day after the election.

Senator Ted Cruz, who is poised to be the only Republican holding statewide office in Texas when Democrats who swept races in the state are sworn in, similarly blamed the war but ultimately joined the majority of his colleagues in voting to block the resolution. He ignored questions from reporters about his decision immediately after the vote.

Senator Todd Young, Republican of Indiana, said that the repeated votes were “unserious” moves by Democrats whom he accused of not considering the effects of immediate withdrawal. It would make sense to have an operational plan for withdrawal after winning the war, he said on Thursday.

When asked whether he believed that the war had been won as the president has repeatedly claimed, he replied, “I don’t think we’ve won.”

Nearly nine months after Mr. Trump launched an attack on Iran without consultation with or authorization by Congress, hostilities continue across the region. Kuwait and Bahrain said on Wednesday that they had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks. Iran said it was targeting American air defense systems in the region. Earlier this month, the United States carried out strikes against Qeshm Island, describing them as defensive operations.

The latest estimate provided to Congress put the war’s costs at $47.1 billion through mid-October.

The vote could be lawmakers’ final opportunity this Congress to limit Mr. Trump’s war powers directly, with little time remaining this year for the House and Senate to move on another such resolution. Some Democrats, however, are pushing to use a year-end spending measure to defund the conflict, thus depriving the administration of the resources it would need to continue waging it.

The measure blocked on Thursday did not have the force of law, but its passage would have amounted to a rebuke of the administration for its conduct of the conflict and for failing to win approval from Congress to wage it.

The last time both chambers passed such a resolution, in June, Mr. Trump berated the Republicans who supported it and ignored the directive.

Control of both chambers will shift in January, when Democrats take control of the House and Senate and gain new tools to challenge Mr. Trump’s ability to carry out the war.

In addition to scheduling more war powers votes, they will be able to advance legislation that restricts military operations and limits spending for the conflict. They will also have the ability to conduct aggressive oversight. But their power will have limits. Most major legislation will require support from Republicans to make it through the Senate, and all bills are subject to a presidential veto.

item.title: Whatever You Thought Texas Was, It’s Bigger and Bluer Than That
item.description:
Texas has long had a particular hold on the national imagination as a place of cowboys and oilmen, of rugged masculinity and conservative politics.

And these days, the Texas brand is among the state’s leading exports, from boots and hats to music and dance. In Texas, state pride runs deep, and the understanding of the state’s identity is considerably more nuanced. But after three decades of Republican control of state government, even Texas Democrats had grown accustomed to the idea that the state was, at its core, conservative.

So when Democrats swept to power in the state this month, winning elections up and down the ballot, it upended assumptions about Texas both inside and outside the state’s borders. And some Texans were left wondering: Is a blue Texas still the Texas they knew?

“I love that this result signals to the rest of the world that there’s no one definition of Texas,” said the “Dazed and Confused” filmmaker Richard Linklater about the blue wave that washed over the state this month. “There never has been.”

Mr. Linklater, a longtime progressive who has never “had a driver’s license anywhere else,” noted that Texas was once reliably blue. It was the home of Lyndon B. Johnson, the Democrat who represented Texas in the Senate before he became president in 1963.

Yet the ties that bind Texans to their home state have always run deeper than politics.

“What distinguishes Texans is that there is an allegiance to the state, not just politically or culturally, but in some kind of deep, profound, spiritual way,” said the Pulitzer Prize-winning writer Lawrence Wright, who has spent decades examining Texas’ culture and identity.

Some of the state’s most prominent conservatives also drew a distinction between its politics and its sense of self. Jim McIngvale, the Houston businessman better known as Mattress Mack and a prominent donor to Republican candidates, said, “The parties of the people leading us changed, but I don’t think the people’s attitude changed, whether D or R.”

Mark Cuban, a minority owner of the Dallas Mavericks and a self-proclaimed independent, tended to agree. Being a Texan, Mr. Cuban said, means “the same as it did” before Election Day.

“Texans, whether you were born here or came here by choice, are and will continue to be proud to be Texans,” said Mr. Cuban, who was born in Pennsylvania and moved to Dallas in the early 1980s.

Others on the right viewed the election results in more troubling terms. When asked about the cultural implications of the election, Robert Jeffress, the senior pastor of First Baptist Dallas and a longtime supporter of President Trump, said he would not read too much into the results of the midterms. But he also invoked the Olivet Discourse, a Bible passage in which Jesus describes signs of the end times.

“He said, in the end, things will gradually unravel,” Mr. Jeffress said. “The slope is downward away from God in our culture, so I think that long-term trend of moving further and further away from God is true for our nation and our world.”

Yet Mr. Jeffress also drew a distinction between his religious identity and what are considered traditional Texan values. His faith came first, he said, adding that the two “are diametrically opposed” at times.

But what exactly constitutes “Texas values” depends largely on whom you ask. Texas is vast — it is home to more than 31 million people and, by land area, it’s bigger than France and almost twice the size of Germany. It’s also one of the most diverse states in America. In Houston, Vietnamese is the third most commonly spoken language in the home. The state is synonymous with oil and gas, but it also generates more renewable energy than any other in the country. In many ways, Texas contradicts its own mythology. It is large; it contains multitudes.

After the Civil War, Texas distanced itself from the Confederacy, leaning into its Western identity instead and remembering the Alamo as a foundational myth. For nearly a century, Texas was effectively a one-party Democratic state. The New Deal would expose divisions within the party, as conservatives became wary of expanding federal power. Those divisions only deepened during the civil rights era; the national Democratic Party’s embrace of equal rights started alienating conservative voters.

As Texas became a Republican stronghold in the 1990s, its conservative reputation overshadowed much of the state’s cultural and political complexity. To the rest of the country, Texas came to symbolize a particular kind of politics.

Even as that conservative image took hold, millions of new people were making Texas their home.

“In terms of the way that Texas looks now, demographically speaking, that’s been in the works for some time,” said Sonia Hernández, a Texas A&M University professor who has written about the Mexican borderlands.

Texas has been among the fastest growing states in the country for several years. The state’s population grew by more than eight million people between 2000 and 2019, with Latinos heavily contributing to that population growth, according to the Texas State Historical Association.

In a state that will now be led by its first Latina governor, Ms. Hernández said it was important to remember Texas’ early history of Tejano leaders, such as José Antonio Navarro, the statesman and rancher who played a role in the state’s independence.

“It’s sort of coming full circle to a certain extent,” she said.

Some of Texas’ cultural leaders, like Mohammed Amer, a Palestinian American comedian who grew up in Houston, have long told stories that challenge the prevailing image of Texas. In his Netflix series “Mo,” he draws on his own experience navigating the American immigration system as a refugee fleeing war in Kuwait. In making the series, Mr. Amer wanted to represent the extraordinary diversity of the city he grew up in — one of the most diverse in the world.

“That’s the Houston that I love, and that’s why I filmed my series here because I felt like it was so wildly underrepresented,” Mr. Amer said. “I want leadership to reflect that.”

In his experience, Texas culture, which he defined as “being kind to your neighbors, having that southern hospitality, believing in God,” has a particular resonance: It reminds him of Arab hospitality. “People probably don’t want me to say that,” he said, laughing.

Mr. Amer put the Houston he knew on screen. And while his affection for Texas has endured, he has grown increasingly alienated by the platforms of its political leadership. In recent years, anti-Muslim rhetoric has become more prominent on the right. “It’s a strange feeling, to love a place so much, and to feel like that place doesn’t love you back,” he said, adding, “The possibility of having new leaders who generally want to protect all Texans — including immigrants and refugees — feels like real work toward rectifying that.”

Mr. Wright wondered what Texans had learned about themselves.

“Was it just one moment in history that we rose up and made this big cultural change?” he asked. “Or was it always the way that people were in Texas, and they were misrepresented by their political leadership?”

He added, “I think we’ve made a discovery about who we are as a people that we didn’t know before.”

item.title: Fire at Railroad Tie Plant in Alabama Closes Schools and Prompts Evacuations
item.description:
A large fire at a facility that recycles railroad ties prompted school closures and evacuations in Attalla, Ala., on Thursday, the authorities said.

The police in Attalla, a city of about 5,800 in Etowah County, about 57 miles northeast of Birmingham, said that residents within a one-mile radius of the fire at the Omaha Track plant should evacuate.

“Please avoid the area and allow emergency personnel to safely respond,” the Attalla Police Department said around 6:30 a.m. Eastern time. About six hours later, the police said that residents could return to their homes but added that roads around the plant would remain closed.

There were no immediate reports of any casualties caused by the fire, and officials did not provide any information on potential causes of the blaze. Company officials, the police, and the fire department could not immediately be reached on Thursday for further details.

Mayor Larry Means of Attalla said that wooden cross ties — which are used to hold steel rails in railroad tracks — were burning, according to WSFA 12. Video broadcast by the TV station showed a thick plume of dark smoke billowing over the area.

Attalla City Schools initially announced on Thursday that schools would open after a two-hour delay, but then announced there would be a complete closure for the entire day. The district’s 1,620 students attend three schools: elementary, middle and high school.

Omaha Track, based in Omaha, processes railroad ties for landscaping, retaining walls, fencing and other uses. Ties are removed from active tracks and processed at its facilities across the United States.

It was not immediately clear how many people work at the facility.

item.title: Fiona the Hippo, Whose Stardom Extended Well Beyond Cincinnati, Has Died
item.description:
Fiona, the hippopotamus who won over the internet in 2017 as zookeepers marked her progress from premature calf to the princess of the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden, died on Thursday. She was 9.

The beloved hippo ate a children’s knit hat about two weeks ago after it accidentally fell into her enclosure. As the zoo attempted a series of procedures to save Fiona, whom veterinarians could not operate on because of her size, her appetite began to diminish.

“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said in a social media post on Thursday. “The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover.”

The Nile hippopotamus was born in the cold of January 2017, six weeks premature. No one expected her to survive. She weighed only 29 pounds (most viable hippos weigh between 55 and 120 pounds at birth) and was kept under constant observation. Every day brought a new health crisis, and every day the team at the Cincinnati Zoo updated a growing legion of fans who cheered on her recovery.

The internet delighted when she loafed, when she farted, when her tank of a body bobbed in the water, when she crashed a wedding proposal. It was Fionamania.

Words like “sassy, unbothered, unproblematic queen” were used to describe a baby hippopotamus without a blink of an eye. Fiona had her own Facebook reality show, and is the subject of a children’s book series.

This is a developing story.

item.title: How to Run a Presidential Bid: Ex-Biden Chief Will Gather Aides of 2028 Hopefuls
item.description:
The strategist who led former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s last two presidential campaigns is organizing a gathering of top aides to several Democrats who are likely to begin running for the White House next year.

The event, set for next month in New York, is being funded in part by the liberal megadonor Alex Soros. It was pitched to the prospective campaign chiefs as a rolling conversation about how to build and maintain the infrastructure for a national political operation.

The private gathering, which was described by nine people briefed on the preparations who spoke on the condition of anonymity, is intended to be far smaller and more private than the 3,000-person convention that Democrats held last week in Denver. It is being convened by Jen O’Malley Dillon, who was the campaign manager for Mr. Biden’s 2020 bid and became the top official overseeing the 2024 campaign for Mr. Biden and then for Vice President Kamala Harris.

The planned event — an unusual gathering in the lead-up to a presidential campaign — shows how Democrats are quietly accelerating their preparations for the 2028 race now that the midterm elections are over.

It is intended to be less a briefing about political strategy or the optimal policy for candidates and more a discussion of the tactics, technology and leadership required for a presidential campaign, the people briefed on the event said. Ms. O’Malley Dillon declined to comment. Mr. Soros could not be reached for comment.

Officials who were invited stressed that the meeting, expected to take place in mid-December, was to be kept secret. One compared it to “Fight Club” — the first rule is do not discuss it — and another said they had been told its existence would not leak to the press.

The invitees included aides for at least eight potential presidential candidates: Ms. Harris, Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland, Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania. Aides for other possible candidates may still be invited later, and other Democratic operatives who are not affiliated with specific politicians are expected to be included as well.

The invitations offer an early indication of whom Democratic presidential candidates might choose to be their top campaign aides once they formalize their White House ambitions.

Those invited include: Eric Hyers, a longtime Beshear aide; Emma Brown, who is expected to lead Mr. Kelly’s campaign if he runs, and Jen Cox, Mr. Kelly’s chief of staff; Brian Fallon, an aide to Ms. Harris; Quentin Fulks, an aide to Mr. Pritzker who has also worked for Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia; Michael Halle, who works for Mr. Buttigieg; and Tim Persico and Dana Fritz, who are expected to help lead Mr. Shapiro’s presidential campaign if he runs.

None of the potential candidates are expected to formally announce a campaign this year, but many of them are laying the groundwork.

On Thursday, former aides to Mr. Buttigieg began a group called Team Pete PAC to encourage him to run for president. Ms. Brown has taken a leave of absence from Giffords, the gun safety group Mr. Kelly founded with his wife, former Representative Gabrielle Giffords, to return to Mr. Kelly’s political orbit before he makes a decision on 2028. A group of progressives created a group called Ready for AOC to urge Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, to run for president.

Some people have said the meeting could be awkward, with officials from rival campaigns-in-waiting gathering to discuss best practices ahead of what is expected to be a crowded and expensive Democratic primary race.

item.title: Agriculture Secretary’s Christian Messages to Staff Went ‘Too Far,’ Judge Says
item.description:
A federal court in California reprimanded Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins on Thursday for Christian religious messages that she had sent to department employees, ruling that they amounted to a violation of the Constitution.

Pointing to the First Amendment’s prohibition on laws “respecting an establishment of religion,” Judge Trina L. Thompson of the U.S. District Court in Northern California limited how Ms. Rollins could promote her religious beliefs in her official duties.

Judge Thompson wrote in a 21-page ruling that “the secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages.” The order said that she must stop “if a colleague asks,” that she could not “create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and that she could not “use official authority to pressure subordinates.”

The judge wrote that Ms. Rollins had gone “too far” when she sent two emails celebrating Christmas and Easter in an explicitly religious manner. In the Christmas email, Ms. Rollins wrote of “our savior Jesus Christ, who came to free us from our sins and open the door to eternal life.” For Easter, Ms. Rollins declared that “he is risen indeed!” and wrote that it was “the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith and the abiding hope of all mankind.”

“From the foot of the cross on Good Friday to the stone rolled away from the now empty tomb, sin has been destroyed,” she continued. “Jesus has been raised from the dead. And God has granted each of us victory and new life. And where there is life — risen life — there is hope.”

Judge Thompson, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., stressed that Ms. Rollins was free to express her religious beliefs to “interested colleagues” and in “appropriate conversations.” She added that she was “keenly aware of the sensitivities present in this action,” and that “this court expresses no view whatsoever on what the secretary can and cannot do in her personal capacity.”

But the judge said Ms. Rollins’s messages, sent through official emails to all department employees, appeared “to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion.”

“Social pressure alone is not state coercion,” Judge Thompson wrote. But, she added, “the totality of the circumstances here demonstrates such immense pressure to amount to coercion.”

Politico reported on the Easter message earlier this year, and the National Federation of Federal Employees, Americans United for Separation of Church and State and seven department workers sued, saying that Ms. Rollins had “adopted a practice of sending increasingly proselytizing communications.”

In a statement, the plaintiffs and their lawyers praised the ruling.

“Federal employees are public servants, not an audience for their bosses’ personal religious beliefs,” said Randy Erwin, the president of the National Federation of Federal Employees. Rachel Laser, the head of Americans United, said the decision “should send a message to the Trump administration that it cannot misuse taxpayer resources to preach” to federal employees.

The Agriculture Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Me, MAGA? Elon Musk Backs Away From a Presidency He Shaped
item.description:
Elon Musk has done a lot for President Trump in the past couple of years.

He spent a cool $290 million to elect him in 2024. He became the wealthiest unelected White House adviser the country had ever known. He spent close to $500 million to help Trump’s allies in the midterms.

Now, though, Musk has a message for the nation: He is not MAGA after all.

That comment came during an interview with my colleague Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook conference yesterday, and I’d encourage you to watch the whole thing. Musk made himself the latest right-leaning cultural figure to distance himself from Trump, following the likes of Joe Rogan and Ben Shapiro.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk said, before trying to downplay his political involvement. “I didn’t put a lot of personal attention into it because I focused on, on building SpaceX, Tesla, you know.”

The intense focus on Musk’s spending obscures an important political point. He was never just a donor on the sidelines, nor a mere MAGA adherent (or “dark gothic MAGA,” as he memorably put it). In the opening months of last year, he was the most visible member of the Trump administration besides the president himself — and Musk’s polarizing and chaotic tenure leading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency became a political liability that the administration struggled to shake.

In other words: It’s not just that Musk failed to help Trump win. It’s that in some ways, he could be part of why Trump’s party lost.

Musk was omnipresent in Washington. His aides gutted government agencies like the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and U.S.A.I.D. He was in the Oval Office with his child on his shoulders; wielding a chain saw onstage at the Conservative Political Action Conference; sitting shotgun in a Tesla with Trump on the White House driveway and — perhaps most controversially — at the Defense Department, meeting with Pete Hegseth.

Polls showed that DOGE was unpopular, as was Musk himself. Even people who voted for Trump weren’t quite sure this was what they had signed up for.

“It was sold to the American people in such a way that, ‘This is going to be good for you,’” Jerry Jacob, a tech worker from New Jersey, told me this fall. He voted for Trump in 2024, but he said he found DOGE off-putting. “Are things better now than before? Honestly, I wouldn’t be able to say yes.”

Democrats seized on the image of Trump cozying up to Musk as they built a caricature of a president beholden to the billionaire class and made it core to their midterm pitch. Musk remained a political target long after he departed the White House in the late spring of 2025. His big spending on behalf of Ken Paxton, the Trump ally and Republican Senate nominee in Texas, gave Democrats a new opening to go after their favorite foil.

“Ken Paxton is funded by one dude,” James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent, said in the closing days of the campaign. “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas.”

“On Nov. 3, we are going to deliver a crystal clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale,” Talarico said. He won convincingly.

Now that the political winds have shifted, Musk has, too. He described himself at DealBook as “ideologically quite moderate,” and praised Texas’ newly elected Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, as “quite moderate” herself.

It was part of his time-honored ritual of cozying up to the powerful, whoever that is. He has showered right-wing leaders in Argentina, India and Brazil with compliments. He took President Barack Obama on a tour of SpaceX in 2010 and said he voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016 before his expensive mission to elect Trump in 2024.

“You know,” he told Andrew, “American elections are not just about money.”

Hannah Fidelman contributed reporting.

item.title: Top White House Cybersecurity Official Steps Down
item.description:
Sean Cairncross, the top cybersecurity official at the White House, is stepping down from his post and leaving the administration, the White House said in a statement on Thursday.

The departure comes as a series of technological outages have plagued major U.S. companies and federal agencies in recent days.

Mr. Cairncross had been the national cyber director, who helps draft the nation’s cyber strategy and coordinates among agencies on cybersecurity, since August 2025. The circumstances of his departure were not immediately clear.

In the past week, technological problems have slowed banking transactions, disrupted email services, shut down a key system at the National Security Agency and temporarily grounded all commercial air traffic in the United States. Officials have said that those episodes were not caused by malicious cyberattacks. But the lack of a clear explanation for some of the outages has contributed to rising public concern.

President Trump has downplayed the outages as minor incidents caused by routine upgrades, asserting that they were “individual events” unrelated to one another.

“It’s life,” Mr. Trump said while traveling in Manila earlier this week. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”Axios earlier reported news of Mr. Craincross’s departure.

As the Trump administration sought to quell rising public worry about the disruptions, Mr. Cairncross did not make public appearances.

Earlier this year, he played a major role in internal administration deliberations related to artificial intelligence safety risks. But he appeared to be increasingly sidelined from those conversations, especially after Mr. Trump in October tapped the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, as the A.I. czar.

Mr. Cairncross was seen by colleagues as close to the former White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles. His office has had a high rate of turnover in recent months, according to former officials. The national cybersecurity director, a position created by Congress, has only indirect authority over A.I. issues.

item.title: Technology Promised Ease. Now It’s Making Many Americans Uneasy.
item.description:
The primary benefit of information technology, Steve Ballmer, the former Microsoft chief executive, said in a speech 20 years ago, “is that it empowers people to do what they want to do.”

For decades, this all-American promise seemed borne out, as rapid advances in technology enabled people to create, communicate and consume with an ease that would have once been unimaginable.

But at some point on the path of inexorable progress, the promise seems to have curdled for a large swath of the population. Rather than feeling empowered by the digital tools they have come to rely on, many are now questioning how powerless they may have actually become.

A seven-day stretch that began last week with a global Microsoft outage affecting email and video calls continued with a succession of tech meltdowns, including the grounding of thousands of flights because of problems with outdated air traffic communications equipment. It was capped by the $2 trillion dollar stock market debut of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, which rocketed an elite few into a new stratosphere of wealth.

Anger had already been building. Well before the series of outages, communities across the country had been pressing for bans on data centers and Flock surveillance cameras, or passing pre-emptive prohibitions on certain kinds of technology, like delivery drones. Schools have banished social media and cellphones, and are facing off with Google over the company’s insistence that classrooms allow A.I.-related products. And the astronomic wealth of tech titans has triggered a ferocious populist reaction, one that partly powered the biggest electoral backlash in generations this month.

And yet the colossal disruptions of this past week have forced people to reckon with how utterly dependent they have become on worldwide computer networks, even before the prospect of the complete A.I. takeover that Silicon Valley power brokers insist is imminent.

As with the period leading up to New Year’s Eve 1999, when experts warned of a potential catastrophic Y2K computing meltdown, Americans in recent days could do little but hope that tech professionals were on top of the problems that could have upended their lives. But even as technology has become far more omnipresent, the techno-optimism at the turn of the new millennium has long faded.

“With Y2K there was this fear that computers are going to become broken,” said Zachary Loeb, a historian of technological disaster at Purdue University who is working on a book on the Y2K scare. “I think in the present there is more of a sense that computers have broken everything.”

The backlash has swelled even as fast-evolving computer technology brings promise along with peril.

Some of the recent outages were triggered when new A.I. tools discovered vulnerabilities and companies rushed to patch them, valuable fixes that brought chaotic side effects. A.I. is making potentially life-changing advances in cancer treatment, while some leading A.I. engineers speak fatalistically of the impending prospect of worldwide unemployment. This week, as fears over computer failures prompted some to start disaster-prepping, others flocked online to try out the blockbuster cultural product of the fall, the video game Grand Theft Auto IV.

As Rabbi Elliott Tepperman sees it, what may have at one point been an intentional bargain — people ceding some control over their daily tasks in return for opportunity and convenience — has become a trap.

“I think we’re way past that bargain,” said Rabbi Tepperman, who in his 2025 Yom Kippur sermon at Bnai Keshet, a synagogue in Montclair, N.J., smashed a smartphone with a hammer. “We’re either addicted or mindlessly giving away our attention for hardly any convenience at all.”

Sixty-nine percent of Americans feel overwhelmed by the number of passwords they have to keep track of, according to the Pew Research Center. Workers at some Fortune 500 companies spend roughly four hours a week — or 5 working weeks a year — toggling between tabs and applications and then having to refocus the brain, according to a 2022 analysis in the Harvard Business Review.

When the trade-off of control for convenience falls short, the problem is more than mere inconvenience. It may be easier to handle personal banking without having to deposit a paycheck at the local branch, but when the bank’s online services fail, the customer discovers that he or she is all but helpless.

“Now that those things are in some ways not working as we’re used to, then we realize how much our agency has sort of been surrendered,” said Bishop Daniel E. Flores of Brownsville, Texas., who was in Baltimore this week for an annual meeting of Catholic bishops, where everyone had to take an early lunch because the digital voting system crashed. “It’s a wake-up moment to re-evaluate how much we — how much do I — want to be dependent.”

Often, the opposition is not to tech itself, but to the sense that it is being foisted on people and communities. In hearing rooms and high school cafeterias around the country, local residents have made the same vociferous objections to data center projects: They are being built not for them, but in the interest of faraway corporations.

“New technology is great,” said Whittney Wood, a D.J. and single mother in central Ohio who narrowly lost a race for state legislature this year in a campaign powered in part by the furious resistance to a local data center. “What I firmly stand against is the big tech people that are shoving these things down our throats, just to make sure that they can get as much profit as possible.”

The sense of futility that runs through these hearings is in some ways belied by the outcomes. Data centers have been successfully blocked in county after county. More than 20 states have introduced or passed bills restricting social media usage among children, though some of these have been challenged in court. And multiple candidates in this year’s midterm elections ran explicitly on platforms of resistance to the power and wealth of big tech — and won.

“A lot of people are feeling like A.I. is just happening to them, and that decisions about this are being made by a fairly small circle of people — and they are responding,” said Kim Daniels, director of the Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life at Georgetown University. “Workers and families and communities need a much bigger place in the conversation.”

In Silicon Valley, there is a growing awareness of the backlash. Technology leaders are offering defenses of their products, even as their companies are defining the new American economy.

Anthropic’s initial public offering prospectus makes the case that artificial intelligence can positively transform society, from potentially curing cancer to already “helping to shorten the lines at the DMV.” It argues that people who buy Anthropic stock should see themselves as “part of something greater,” not simply as making a “transactional” purchase.

Yet there is broad talk in A.I. circles of the “gradual disempowerment of humans,” said Ruxandra Teslo, a science writer who recently posted a much-discussed essay about “handoverism,” the idea circulating in Silicon Valley that humanity should — or will soon be forced to — cede control of civilization to a benevolent A.I.

“For the first time in Silicon Valley, increasing human agency doesn’t seem to even be the stated goal,” she said.

Not everyone in the tech world is enthusiastic about this, she said, but many are resigned to it. The way some discuss the scenario suggests that they, too, feel powerless, unable to curb the development of a technology that they believe is leading in a very grim direction.

“I’ve seen some people even welcome the fact that there is a backlash,” Ms. Teslo said. “They want someone to stop them from making these systems. Because they feel like they cannot stop themselves.”

Yair Rosenberg contributed reporting.

item.title: California Thieves Carried Out String of Train Heists, Prosecutors Say
item.description:
The train robberies outlined in the 49-page indictment read like a Hollywood treatment for a Wild West-meets-the-A.I.-age heist movie.

Over more than two years, prosecutors say, a crew of 14 people carried out a series of freight train heists in Southern California, boarding the slow-moving trains in early-morning darkness. After sawing their way into boxcars stuffed with sneakers and electronics, they forced the trains to a stop, filled waiting getaway vans with the goods and fled to stash houses, according to the grand jury indictment unsealed on Thursday.

The thieves were as meticulous in documenting their exploits as they were in planning them, according to the indictment, which includes images from a video showing one of the accused using a circular saw to cut the lock of a train car, sparks flying. In some instances, those charged had posted videos of their crimes to social media, officials said.

The group called themselves the “Los Trenes” — Spanish for “The Trains,” according to prosecutors. In an Instagram chat described in the indictment, the crew members shared A.I.-generated images of black-clad men in black BMWs driving alongside a train as their accomplices unload boxes of Nike shoes.

Over more than two years, prosecutors say, their take was staggering: more than $22 million worth of Nike, Hoka and Crocs shoes, as well as electronics and power tools. Altogether, the crew plundered more than three dozen train cars, officials said.

Law enforcement officers on Thursday fanned out across Southern California to make arrests.

The charges followed a 14-month task force investigation, named Operation CoolKicks, that involved numerous agencies, including the Los Angeles Police Department, the Department of Justice, the Los Angeles District Attorney’s Office, Homeland Security Investigations and the Union Pacific Railroad police.

Jim McDonnell, chief of the Los Angeles Police Department, said at a news conference on Thursday that the indictment “marks the largest property crime bust in L.A.P.D. and railroad history.”

“This is much more than a modern-day train robbery,” he said. “It was a highly coordinated operation that disrupted our nation’s supply chain.”

The indictment charged 14 men with 17 felony counts related to the heists, and they face decades in prison if convicted, according to the Justice Department. It was unclear whether any of the men charged had legal representation.

Southern California is a hub for America’s supply chain, with goods arriving by sea at two ports, Los Angeles and Long Beach, where they are then loaded onto trains bound for warehouses around the country. In recent years, trains, especially in the Los Angeles area, have been targeted by thieves with greater frequency, and law enforcement has devoted more resources to countering the crimes.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” said Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, whose office is prosecuting the case. Mr. Essayli posted a video on X of the man prosecutors say was the crew’s ringleader sawing off a lock on a train car.

“I encourage criminals to film themselves while committing crimes,” Mr. Essayli said at the news conference. “It makes our jobs a lot easier.”

The robbery crew had their own network of stash houses and warehouses across the region, according to the indictment. Once the looted goods were safely stored, they arranged to sell the products to buyers who would then resell them to the public. One company, a sneaker reseller identified only as “Company 1” in the indictment, operated a warehouse in Santa Monica, Calif., and paid more than $1 million over the last two years for stolen Nikes, prosecutors say.

The indictment describes a series of train heists from February of 2024 until this summer. The goods had been on their way to places all around the country, including Indiana, Texas, Kansas and Pennsylvania.

Each heist involved several men, with some jumping onboard the moving freight trains, which were as much as three miles long. Other members of the crew, using rented vans and trucks, positioned themselves ahead of the train’s route at an agreed-upon, often remote and isolated, location. Once the train reached that spot, one of the men on board would cut the hose supplying air to the brakes, “forcing the trains to come to an emergency stop,” prosecutors wrote.

Once the getaway vehicles were stuffed with sneakers or tools or electronics, the goods would be stored at stash houses while the men arranged transactions with resellers.

Well before the arrests this week, the crew had hints that law enforcement officers were on their tail.

According to the indictment, an unnamed co-conspirator sent a text to one of the defendants saying he had been arrested for receiving stolen property. He wrote that he “could have easily thru your name under the bus.”

The last robbery detailed in the indictment was on Aug. 6. The man prosecutors say was the leader of the operation boarded a train and discovered an especially valuable stash of unreleased Nike Air Jordan “Space Jam” sneakers.

Prosecutors say he texted a photograph to the group chat. “No way,” one of the members replied. “Sheeeesh,” wrote another.

item.title: Justice Department Gives Up on Alaska Senate Lawsuit
item.description:
The Trump administration is giving up its bid to block the certification of results in Alaska’s Senate race, abandoning a legal maneuver that threatened to prevent Senator-elect Mary Peltola, a Democrat, from taking office.

The Justice Department asked a federal court to declare its lawsuit against Alaska moot on Thursday, two days after The Associated Press called the competitive race for Ms. Peltola.

Democrats helped recruit a second candidate with a name similar to that of the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, The New York Times reported. On President Trump’s order, the Justice Department had argued even before Election Day, and before The Times’s report, that Alaska should not certify a narrow victory for Ms. Peltola until it could be determined that her win was not due to voter confusion.

But critics called the move legally meritless, and lawyers for the state of Alaska, where Republicans control the governorship and the Legislature, sought to have the case dismissed.

Ms. Peltola ended up winning by more than four percentage points, a wide enough margin that Mr. Sullivan would still have lost even if every ballot cast for the lesser-known candidate had gone to him.

In a court filing on Thursday, the Justice Department maintained that its initial bid had merit, but it conceded that it would be impossible for its lawyers to interrogate voters about their reasoning now that ballots had been de-identified. Lawyers for the Justice Department “reluctantly” acknowledged that “there no longer exists any means” to figure out whether voters for the potential spoiler, Dan J. Sullivan, meant to pick the incumbent senator instead, and therefore no way to vindicate its claims.

A judge denied the Trump administration’s request to segregate ballots cast for Dan J. Sullivan ahead of the election, but the Justice Department appealed.

The judge could still rule on the merits of the case, even though the Justice Department argues the point is moot.

In October, the Justice Department announced it was investigating Democrats who recruited a decoy Alaska Senate candidate over potential illegal activity. Thursday’s filings did not address the status of that inquiry, which prosecutors acknowledged might never yield criminal charges.

The Justice Department sent letters to 20 Democrats informing them that they might be targets or asking them to preserve their records, and issued hundreds of subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Ms. Peltola has claimed she was unaware of the plan to recruit a spoiler.

Mr. Sullivan’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a statement responding to Thursday’s filing, Ms. Peltola said that “voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in” and added that she was eager to “get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.”

“For Alaskans, there is only one direction: forward,” she said.

Kellen Browning contributed reporting from Anchorage and Devlin Barrett from Washington.
