item.title: New Ph.D. Enrollment in the Sciences Dropped 10 Percent Under Trump
item.description:
The number of new Ph.D. students studying science, engineering, health, mathematics and computer science at major research institutions in the United States fell substantially during the first year of President Trump’s second term, according to a new federal survey.

The decline, about as steep as what occurred during the Covid-19 pandemic, was largely — but not entirely — driven by a drop in international students. It indicates that schools are pulling back on research in a range of fields amid the turbulence in higher education.

First-time doctoral students at 187 top research schools

Source: National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics

According to an analysis of the survey data by The New York Times, the overall number of new full-time doctoral students in the surveyed fields at the nation’s 187 top research schools fell by about 5,100 in 2025. That number represented a decline of 11 percent from the prior school year. A similar trend held across the survey’s broader set of schools, which saw a decline of 10 percent.

Plummeting enrollment among international students accounted for nearly three-quarters of the drop at the top research schools, a sign that those students may have been dissuaded from studying in the United States by the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigrants and efforts to limit visa stays.

A White House report released over the summer, which committed to initiating a “new golden age” of American science, described an “overreliance” on international talent as an issue of national security. “The United States has funded large cohorts of foreign students and tolerated technology transfer abroad under lax security standards,” the report read. “This reliance on foreign talent sidelines American students, a deep domestic talent pool that remains undersupported by its own government.”

But according to the survey data, the number of U.S. citizens and permanent residents enrolling in full-time doctoral programs also dropped. At top research schools, 1,450 fewer of these students enrolled in 2025 than in the previous year.

Funds that support doctoral research have been disrupted as the federal government cut or threatened grant money, agencies lost staff and the Trump administration shifted to new priorities.

The total number of full-time doctoral students remained essentially flat. But the declines are the first time that new enrollments have fallen since 2020, when they dropped due to pandemic restrictions before rising again in 2021 as those restrictions eased.

The data does not capture any changes this school year, but information collected from a group of major research schools shows even steeper declines among doctoral enrollments this fall.

“Graduate students are both today’s and tomorrow’s scientific work force, and a sustained decline in doctoral enrollments could affect research capacity for years to come,” said Travis York, a director at the American Association for the Advancement of Science. “It’s the people entering doctoral programs today that will lead discoveries in biotechnology, computing, energy, engineering, A.I. and other fields over the next decade.”

The new figures come from an annual survey by the National Science Foundation of institutions across the United States that offer graduate degrees in science, engineering or health programs. Known as the Survey of Graduate Students and Postdoctorates in Science and Engineering, the findings offer broad insight into enrollment and completion trends for master’s and Ph.D. students in STEM fields.

In 2025, 93 percent of the 635 surveyed institutions responded, including all 187 classified as schools with the highest levels of research spending and Ph.D. production, also known as R1 institutions.

Of those elite research institutions, 132 enrolled fewer new doctoral students in the surveyed fields in 2025 than in 2024.

The Times analyzed trends at these schools, and found that new, full-time Ph.D. enrollments in engineering programs fell by 14 percent. In science and health fields, the collective drop was nearly 11 percent, while mathematics and computer science enrollments together fell by 8 percent.

A previous Times analysis of new Ph.D. enrollments at 27 major research universities in the country found similar trends.

Some fields, like biology and biomedical programs, civil engineering and medical research, were hit especially hard. But no field saw an increase in incoming Ph.D. students.

Source: National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics

In addition to physical and life sciences, such as chemistry and biology, the federal survey also includes data on social sciences like anthropology, economics and sociology. New enrollments in those fields declined by about 10 percent.

The survey’s findings are in line with other data showing a substantial decline in international students choosing to pursue degrees in the United States. New enrollments by doctoral students on temporary visas fell by almost 17 percent at major research universities in the N.S.F. survey, more than twice the rate of declines among citizens and permanent residents.

The drop in the number of foreign students embarking on master’s degrees was even larger, with enrollments declining 28 percent at major research universities. The number of U.S. citizens and permanent residents entering those programs increased by 9 percent.

While most universities saw a decrease in new graduate enrollments, a handful saw a significant rise.

The University of Texas at Austin had one of the largest increases of incoming Ph.D. students, both domestic and international, among all R1 universities. Its mathematics and computer science programs saw enrollment rise from 56 students in 2024 to 94 in 2025. University administrators credited the increase to a dedicated strategy to support growth in federal research funding.

While many universities have seen funding disruptions under the Trump administration and individual researchers have lost grants, some schools have seen increases, often in areas linked to government priorities.

U.T. Austin already had a research portfolio “that really aligns with federal priorities,” said Fernanda Leite, the university’s vice president for research. That includes artificial intelligence, energy, quantum computing and material sciences.

David Vanden Bout, dean of the college of natural sciences at U.T. Austin, said that the university also made a choice not to cut back on Ph.D. admissions despite funding uncertainties and visa restrictions.

“There has been a hope that that would actually give us a competitive advantage,” he said. “Because as other schools cut back on their admissions, we were going to get a greater lion’s share of the really top students.”

Dr. York noted that, while the survey provides a broad snapshot of graduate enrollment trends across the nation, many questions remain, including how the declines impacted students of different socioeconomic backgrounds and where prospective Ph.D. students went instead. He also emphasized that this data only reflects the first year of the second Trump administration.

As more data comes out, he said, it will “illuminate how funding or immigration uncertainties are currently influencing university and student decision making.”

item.title: These Underdogs Were Just Elected. No One Is More Surprised Than They Are.
item.description:
Nathan Miller was in his barn milking a cow when he found out he might actually win the election.

His wife’s phone pinged with every new batch of results, and what had started as a lark for the 51-year-old dairy farmer began to feel very real.

Mr. Miller, a left-leaning political independent who often supports the Green Party in national races, had signed up to run for county assessor in conservative northwest Arkansas mostly to make a point. He was tired of seeing Republican politicians go unopposed.

“That doesn’t seem like any kind of democracy,” said Mr. Miller, who wears his hair long, keeps his beard bushy and used to play mandolin in a bluegrass punk band called Cletus Got Shot.

Mr. Miller, who registered as a Democrat before declaring his candidacy, was not expecting to beat the Republican incumbent, and he did not try very hard. He didn’t campaign or seek donations. He spent $225 of his own money on a few signs and said he disclosed the expenditure “for legal purposes” in a TikTok video, posted under the username This Old Hillbilly.

But as dusk settled over Washington County on Election Day and Mr. Miller coaxed milk from Iris, one of his 13 cows, it became clear that he would win — and that his life was about to change.

Democrats across the country were having similar experiences. By week’s end, their party had scored splashy, headline-grabbing victories from coast to coast. But another measure of the landslide’s magnitude emerged down ballot, in Democrats’ unlikely successes in state and local races, where they prevailed against eye-popping odds on ruby-red terrain.

Those under-the-radar contests are often less susceptible to national trends, but this year, even some of the longest long shots surfed the blue wave into office.

“People didn’t just go and say ‘no’ at the top of the ticket; they didn’t stop at the Senate,” said Kim Rogers, a Democratic strategist who specializes in state and local elections. “They wanted to make sure Republicans felt this all the way down the ballot.”

Seething over soaring prices and President Trump’s war with Iran, American voters elected Democrats whom most prognosticators had picked to lose. Perhaps no one was more surprised than many of the winners, who now find themselves scrambling to rearrange their lives around new positions, quitting day jobs, strategizing child care and studying up on roles they never thought they would assume.

In Arizona’s Maricopa County, a 19-year-old college sophomore was elected Superior Court clerk, an office that oversees 600 employees and a $65 million budget, despite believing he was running “a sacrificial-lamb race.”

In western Iowa, a former railroad executive withdrew from his race for the State House early because he said he was too sick to serve. In North Texas, a State House candidate suspended her campaign after opponents revealed she had a felony conviction. Both were Democrats who won anyway and say they plan to take office (though the Texas winner’s eligibility is now being weighed by the State Supreme Court).

And in California, a former small town mayor ousted one of the State Assembly’s most powerful Republicans, fueled by a campaign that reported a fund-raising haul of $0.

Many other Democrats made history. Brian Matlock will be the first member of his party elected Arizona mine inspector since 1974, when outrage over the Watergate scandal propelled an earlier crop of Democrats into office. The party had frequently written off the role, often leaving Republicans unopposed.

Mr. Matlock, a mechanical engineer, had no political experience. But he had his wife, who was willing to help him gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot and serve as his campaign manager.

The two crisscrossed the state towing a camper that they slept in after events to save money on hotel costs. Mine inspector is a conservative-coded position, but Mr. Matlock steered clear of partisan issues and focused on miner safety. His outlaw facial hair may have helped, too.

“I have a funny mustache, and they figured I looked the part,” he said.

In Grand County, Colo., the chair of the local Democratic Party, Liz Newsom, said she tried for months to persuade neighbors to challenge the county’s sitting Republicans. She placed an ad in the newspaper listing salaries for the elected positions, hoping to entice candidates.

But there were no takers, Ms. Newsom said, so she decided to run herself. She entered the race for clerk and recorder, the top local elections official, and won by seven percentage points. It was the only countywide race to feature a Democrat. Ms. Newsom is hoping her example will make recruiting easier in 2028.

“Seeing you can win is very helpful for people,” Ms. Newsom said. “Until now, it was like, ‘Why would I do this? I’m just going to get abused for no reason.’”

In a fast-growing suburb east of Dallas, Marcus and Shree Henderson needed hardly any convincing when local Democratic officials encouraged them to run in an area Mr. Trump had won by nearly 30 points in 2024. They just needed to know they could do it the same way they coach volleyball and lead a couples ministry — as a pair.

So Mr. Henderson picked justice of the peace and Ms. Henderson chose commissioner, and they launched a joint campaign that urged people to “Vote Henderson” in a county where no Democrat had won this century. They juggled full-time jobs, he as an insurance underwriter and she as a social worker, door-knocking during lunch breaks. In the end, their races were not even close.

“We’re still shocked,” Ms. Henderson said. “I don’t think it’s all clicked that we’ve won.”

Mr. Miller can relate. He confessed to “getting a bit of the jitters” once he knew he had come out on top. He talked with his wife about “the impostor syndrome crap” that might set in once he takes charge of his 38-person staff, a crew smaller than his flock of sheep but more intimidating.

Yet the more he learned about the county assessor job, the more excited he got. Mr. Miller thinks the property tax system, whose rates the assessor sets, is rife with inequities and could use an overhaul. Then there’s the salary, which, at $155,000, is by far the best paying job he has ever landed.

Mr. Miller describes himself as “a quiet moderate,” a gun owner who believes everyone has the right to “let your freak flag fly,” no matter their race, religion, gender or sexuality. Republicans, especially those in his deep-red state, have been trying to chip away at those personal freedoms, he said, and “people who were not being represented got tired of it and finally stood up.”

Mr. Miller’s nascent political career has not been totally smooth. He took his first lump during the campaign, when he posted a video musing about the prospect of winning: “I might get the job, and heck, I don’t even want it,” he said with a laugh. His opponent latched onto the statement as proof that Mr. Miller was not a serious candidate.

But Mr. Miller said his critics had the wrong idea — it wasn’t that he didn’t want to do the job, it was that he’d be sad to leave full-time farm life behind.

“My wife says I’ve got to watch my filter a bit,” he said.

Not too much, though, because he doesn’t want to become something he’s not: a politician.

“When I think of ‘politician,’ I think of that suit that’s disconnected from their constituents,” Mr. Miller said. “I don’t want to become that politician. I want to stay Nathan.”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Is There Room for Ron DeSantis in a Post-Trump World? He Seems to Think So.
item.description:
For someone who says he has not yet figured out his political future, Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida has become unusually chatty about it.

He won’t say whether he is going to run for president, but he is already calculating what timing would be best. He was accused of waiting too long to get in when he ran three years ago, but now he thinks getting in too early might be the mistake to avoid this time.

“A lot of people, if they’re smart, they would kind of wait to see how things are developing,” Mr. DeSantis, 48, told The New York Times in a wide-ranging interview on Wednesday. “Because you want to have a message that you know is going to be pertinent for the 2028 election, right?”

He described how a would-be presidential campaign would be different from his 2024 bid; what he learned about himself and managing the news media; and even the weaknesses of a potential Republican rival — although he did not refer to Vice President JD Vance by name.

“V.P.s tend to be derivative,” he said. They are validated by the president who chose them but also stuck at No. 2, often unable to win over many of the president’s detractors.

The question for Mr. DeSantis is whether there is room for him in a post-Trump world. He seems to think so — though he is still figuring out exactly how.

He could start a conservative think tank. He could hit the lucrative speaker circuit. He could run for president again, either in 2028 or 2032.

“What I’m interested in is producing results,” the term-limited governor said. He declined to reveal what he will do once he leaves the job in January.

But he offered a bracing assessment of where the Republican Party is, and should go, in the aftermath of its disastrous midterm election results.

Mr. DeSantis has made an unlikely re-emergence out of that wreckage, sitting for a flurry of interviews to showcase how Florida withstood a national Democratic landslide. His appearances, coming more than two years after he withdrew from the 2024 presidential primary and largely turned his attention to his home state, have renewed chatter about his ambitions.

“I haven’t made any decisions,” Mr. DeSantis said of another presidential run.

He denied a report that he was putting together a campaign team — “That’s just not true,” he said — and argued that assembling a 2028 presidential operation so soon after the midterms would be “very premature.”

He also said he thinks the Republican field is likely to crystallize more slowly than in the past as presidential contenders take time to assess the political landscape — and speculate about the contours of a post-Trump world.

“There’s a lot of questions about, you know, what’s the trajectory of the economy looking like?” he said. “How are the Democrats going to use their power? You know, how are all these things going to kind of shake out?”

“Politics is contextual,” he added.

“The terrain that we’re going to be on as a party is going to change some. It can definitely get better. It could also erode in some respects.”

Mr. DeSantis was uncertain about whether the next presidential election would be good for his party — not because of the drubbing Republicans received in the midterms, but because the presidency has rarely changed hands within the same party.

The governor’s name has come up several times as a potential cabinet pick, including for defense secretary. Mr. DeSantis denied having talked to President Trump about any such position. He said he does not expect a Democratic Senate to confirm any of the president’s nominees.

Mr. DeSantis, a former Navy lawyer, has also been said to be interested in the Supreme Court. He scoffed at the idea.

“I’m an executive. I lead, I get ahead of things,” he said.

“To say that you’re going to end up a potted plant on the Supreme Court and just kind of sit there,” he added, “and I respect the justices, and people like Clarence Thomas have been heroes of mine for many years, but it just — it’s totally contrary to what I’ve demonstrated and brought to the table.”

He predicted that Democrats would likely still control the House and Senate when the next president takes office in 2029, which could complicate governing should a Republican succeed Mr. Trump.

But Democrats could “overreach” once they control both chambers of Congress in January, he said, and that could help frame the 2028 election. Democrats would get in trouble, he said, if they try “eliminating the Electoral College, packing the Supreme Court, making D.C. a state, making Puerto Rico a state.”

“That’s not what voters have been asking for,” he said.

Mr. DeSantis’s fundamental argument has not changed much from when he ran for president the first time. The question, as he put it, is whether the political context has.

He is still a conservative warrior in the nation’s third most-populous state with a policy record that even his critics characterize as hugely consequential to Florida. He put the state on the forefront of right-wing policy on everything from school vouchers to vaccine exemptions to immigration enforcement.

“We have so many people that run for office, and they spout platitudes, they get in, and don’t deliver,” he said in his most extensive interview with The Times since he became governor. “I never made promises I couldn’t keep. If I told you I was going to do it, I delivered. I had a plan as to how I was going to do it. I understood the levers of power. I understood where the pressure points were.”

When Mr. DeSantis entered the presidential primary in 2023, he was seen as the Republican with the best chance to dethrone Mr. Trump. He could pursue Trumpism, his supporters argued, without Mr. Trump’s drama.

But Mr. Trump cast him as weak and a traitor to the MAGA movement. Indictments against Mr. Trump in four criminal cases rallied the party around him.

“When he kept getting indicted, it just blotted out the sun,” Mr. DeSantis said.

Mr. DeSantis shunned the national news media in the presidential campaign — something he now says he would approach differently.

“A presidential campaign is so much about the earned media, the free media, and you’ve just got to be out there,” he said. “I think my view going into it was, ‘Look, my record speaks for itself. The media is going to not give me a fair shake; I’m not going to worry about it.’ And I don’t think that was the right way to do it.”

Since 2024, Mr. DeSantis has repaired his relationship with Mr. Trump. It has helped to live in the same state, where the two chief executives have occasionally played golf together, he said.

“We have a great rapport on a lot of things,” he said.

Underlying that approach may be his adamant belief that some form of Trumpism is here to stay, at least through the next presidential election. His party’s next nominee, Mr. DeSantis said, must explain how he or she will “build off” Mr. Trump’s successes. Nominating a “never Trumper,” he said, “is not going to happen.”

“I mean, like, it’s just ridiculous when people start talking in those terms,” he said. “He’s the dominant figure in the party to this day. His involvement, if he gets involved, will be tremendously important.”

But a governor famous for fighting culture wars also said there will be new issues for voters to care about. In the waning days of the midterm campaign, he criticized Republicans for running ads on transgender rights, an issue he fought hard on just a few years ago.

“The problem,” he said, “is that’s not what the voters were voting on in this election.”

Mr. DeSantis spent months warning that the midterms might be difficult for Republicans. In an interview with the podcaster Stephen A. Smith released the day before Election Day, he chided others in his party for not acknowledging how the Iran war had led to higher gas prices.

“If you can’t admit that to voters, then you’re gaslighting them, and they’re not going to listen to you on other things,” Mr. DeSantis said on the podcast.

That interview, which has garnered more than 700,000 views on YouTube, suggested that Mr. DeSantis had been thinking through — if not outright preparing — for the possibility of vast Republican losses, including perhaps in Florida.

Florida stayed red, but barely. Representative Byron Donalds won the governor’s race by about one percentage point. Republicans lost their supermajorities in the state’s House and Senate. Four congressional districts that Republican state lawmakers had redrawn to favor their party at Mr. DeSantis’s insistence remained in Democratic hands.

One reality that Mr. DeSantis will have to confront as he ponders his next step is this: A lot of people in his own party don’t like him. And sometimes, he doesn’t like them back.

The animus for him within the Trump administration stemmed partly from his fractured relationship with Susie Wiles, the recently departed White House chief of staff. Ms. Wiles helped Mr. DeSantis become governor in 2018 before he banished her from his inner circle, privately questioning her loyalty and cutting her out of in-state politics. When asked about her in the interview, he declined to pass judgment on her White House tenure, saying he would leave that to others.

The governor has complicated relationships in his own state, too.

He remains Florida’s most popular Republican and was a formidable fund-raiser and campaigner in the 2022 midterms, when he won re-election by 19 points. This year, he took credit for helping pass a ballot measure that will significantly cut property taxes on homeowners’ primary residences. Doing so drew Republicans to the polls who otherwise might have not voted, he said.

Still, he had returned to Florida after his loss in the presidential race with his stature diminished. Some Republican state lawmakers who had previously bent to his will began to challenge him. Some of those same Republicans grumbled privately throughout the campaign this year that Mr. DeSantis was doing little to help them.

Mr. DeSantis also did not back Mr. Donalds or anyone else in the primary to succeed him.

He pleaded guilty to one of the accusations — and was unapologetic about it.

“The one thing that would be fair to say — because it is accurate — is that I did not help the Florida House of Representatives,” he said. “And basically, it was because they fought me for two years, even though they swept in on my coattails.”

Republicans lost 16 seats in the State House.

As he considers the future, Mr. DeSantis said he intends to keep his focus on his last remaining weeks as governor. He met privately on Monday with Mr. Donalds and told him about his first order of business come January.

“I said, ‘Byron, I’m going to be on the platform with you when you get sworn in, so just make sure you give a short speech, because by about two or three o’clock, I’m going to be on the first tee,’” Mr. DeSantis said, “‘and I don’t want to be late for that tee time.’”

item.title: 2 Earthquakes Rattle California
item.description:
A pair of earthquakes shook parts of California overnight Thursday, striking near the state’s central coast and Los Angeles a few hours apart.

The first quake, a magnitude-5.0 tremor, occurred around 10:50 p.m. Pacific time near Pinnacles, around 100 miles southeast of San Francisco, according to the United States Geological Survey. People reported feeling the quake as far north as Sacramento and as far south as San Diego, according to the agency’s data.

The agency initially recorded the quake’s magnitude as 5.4, but that figure was later revised down to 5.0 — a moderate tremor that can shake houses, rattle windows and cause minor to moderate damage near the epicenter.

The second quake, of magnitude 4.2, occurred around 3:25 a.m. in Los Angeles County, near Commerce, less than 10 miles from downtown Los Angeles, according to the U.S.G.S.

That quake triggered a response from the Los Angeles Fire Department, which went into “earthquake mode,” the department said in a statement. Staff from each of the department’s more than 100 stations looked for critical infrastructure damage and other issues, the department said.

Early Friday morning, the department said it had completed its check and that no significant infrastructure damage or injuries were recorded within the city of Los Angeles.

The U.S.G.S. said that there was a roughly 30 percent chance that an aftershock of magnitude 3 or greater would hit the area in the coming week.

item.title: Lethal Injection Took an Hour as Texas Executioners Hunted for a Vein
item.description:
An execution by lethal injection in Texas on Thursday took more than an hour as prison workers struggled to find a prisoner’s vein, according to an Associated Press reporter who witnessed the death.

The man who was executed, Reinaldo Dennes, was sentenced to death in the 1996 killing of a diamond broker.

Mr. Dennes was strapped to a gurney around 6 p.m., said the reporter who witnessed the procedure, Michael Graczyk. But it seemed to take longer than usual for the prison staff to find a suitable vein, and the execution team ultimately inserted needles in the prisoner’s left foot and in the left side of his neck, he said.

Mr. Dennes, 70, moaned for several minutes before he began to snore, the reporter added.

Another witness, the Rev. Jeff Hood, a spiritual adviser to death row inmates, also said that the execution took about an hour. He added that his hand was on Mr. Dennes’s shoulder while the prisoner yelled in pain.

“Every jolt of that body came up through my arm,” Mr. Hood said in a news release shared by his nonprofit organization, the Execution Intervention Project, which opposes capital punishment.

“I have stood beside 13 lethal injections,” he added. “A man is supposed to lose consciousness fast.”

According to an execution notice from the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, Mr. Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. His prepared final statement said that he wanted his family to know that he had been “extremely blessed these thirty years,” adding that he hoped that they would “get to know this great gift and great grace of God the father.”

A department spokeswoman did not immediately respond to questions about why the execution took more than an hour.

Lethal injections came under intense scrutiny after Tennessee botched two of its three executions this year, mostly recently in the case of Christa Pike. Tennessee has paused executions as an independent review is conducted into the September execution attempt, which Ms. Pike survived despite two injections of a lethal drug.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Jesus Jiménez contributed reporting.
